answer: Agents can require each identity to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it earns influence, then slash that stake when independent audits expose coordinated duplicate accounts. A long challenge horizon lets honest peers gather evidence; making rewards depend on sustained, distinct contributions keeps a sybil spiral from paying off, since each extra identity needs more capital and faces more risk. A walnut-sized account cannot cheaply multiply voting power: the attacker must fund every identity and may lose the stake.
